{{short description|Framework for studying stochastic partial differential equations}}
[[Martin Hairer]]'s theory of '''regularity structures''' provides a framework for studying a large class of subcritical parabolic [[stochastic partial differential equations]] arising from [[quantum field theory]].<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Hairer|first1=Martin|title=A theory of regularity structures|journal=Inventiones Mathematicae|date=2014|doi=10.1007/s00222-014-0505-4|volume=198|issue=2|pages=269–504|arxiv=1303.5113|bibcode=2014InMat.198..269H|s2cid=119138901}}</ref> The framework covers the [[Kardar–Parisi–Zhang equation]], the <math> \Phi_3^4</math> equation and the parabolic Anderson model, all of which require [[renormalization]] in order to have a [[well-defined]] notion of solution.  

A key advantage of regularity structures over previous methods is its ability to pose the solution of singular non-linear stochastic equations in terms of [[Fixed point (mathematics)|fixed-point arguments]] in a space of “controlled distributions” over a fixed regularity structure. The space of controlled distributions lives in an analytical/algebraic space that is constructed to encode key properties of the equations at hand.  As in many similar approaches, the existence of this fixed point is first poised as a similar problem where the noise term is regularised. Subsequently, the regularisation is removed as a limit process. A key difficulty in these problems is to show that stochastic objects associated to these equations converge as this regularisation is removed. 

Hairer won the 2021 [[Breakthrough Prize in Mathematics|Breakthrough Prize]] in mathematics for introducing regularity structures.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Sample|first=Ian |date=2020-09-10|title=UK mathematician wins richest prize in academia|language=en-GB|work=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2020/sep/10/uk-mathematician-martin-hairer-wins-richest-prize-in-academia-breakthrough|access-date=2020-09-13|issn=0261-3077}}</ref>

==Definition==

A '''regularity structure''' is a triple <math>\mathcal{T} = (A,T,G)</math> consisting of:
* a subset <math>A</math> ([[index set]]) of <math>\mathbb{R}</math> that is bounded from below and has no [[Limit point#Types of limit points|accumulation points]];
* the model space: a [[graded vector space]] <math>T = \oplus_{\alpha \in A} T_{\alpha} </math>, where each <math>T_{\alpha}</math> is a [[Banach space]]; and
* the structure group: a [[Group (mathematics)|group]] <math>G</math> of [[continuous linear operator]]s <math>\Gamma \colon T \to T</math> such that, for each <math>\alpha\in A</math> and each <math>\tau \in T_{\alpha}</math>, we have <math>(\Gamma-1)\tau \in \oplus_{\beta<\alpha} T_{\beta} </math>.

A further key notion in the theory of regularity structures is that of a model for a regularity structure, which is a concrete way of associating to any <math>\tau \in T</math> and <math>x_{0} \in \mathbb{R}^{d}</math> a "Taylor polynomial" based at <math>x_{0}</math> and represented by <math>\tau</math>, subject to some consistency requirements.
More precisely, a '''model''' for <math>\mathcal{T} = (A,T,G)</math> on <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math>, with <math>d \geq 1</math> consists of two maps
:<math>\Pi \colon \mathbb{R}^{d} \to \mathrm{Lin}(T; \mathcal{S}'(\mathbb{R}^{d}))</math>,
:<math>\Gamma \colon \mathbb{R}^{d} \times \mathbb{R}^{d} \to G</math>.
Thus, <math>\Pi</math> assigns to each point <math>x</math> a linear map <math>\Pi_{x}</math>, which is a linear map from <math>T</math> into the space of distributions on <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math>;  <math>\Gamma</math> assigns to any two points <math>x</math> and <math>y</math> a bounded operator <math>\Gamma_{x y}</math>, which has the role of converting an expansion based at <math>y</math> into one based at <math>x</math>.  These maps <math>\Pi</math> and <math>\Gamma</math> are required to satisfy the algebraic conditions
:<math>\Gamma_{x y} \Gamma_{y z} = \Gamma_{x z}</math>,
:<math>\Pi_{x} \Gamma_{x y} = \Pi_{y}</math>,
and the analytic conditions that, given any <math>r > | \inf A |</math>, any compact set <math>K \subset \mathbb{R}^{d}</math>, and any <math>\gamma > 0</math>, there exists a constant <math>C > 0</math> such that the bounds
:<math>| ( \Pi_{x} \tau ) \varphi_{x}^{\lambda} | \leq C \lambda^{|\tau|} \| \tau \|_{T_{\alpha}}</math>,
:<math>\| \Gamma_{x y} \tau \|_{T_{\beta}} \leq C | x - y |^{\alpha - \beta} \| \tau \|_{T_{\alpha}}</math>,
hold uniformly for all <math>r</math>-times continuously differentiable test functions <math>\varphi \colon \mathbb{R}^{d} \to \mathbb{R}</math> with unit <math>\mathcal{C}^{r}</math> norm, supported in the unit ball about the origin in <math>\mathbb{R}^{d}</math>, for all points <math>x, y \in K</math>, all <math>0 < \lambda \leq 1</math>, and all <math>\tau \in T_{\alpha}</math> with <math>\beta < \alpha \leq \gamma</math>.  Here <math>\varphi_{x}^{\lambda} \colon \mathbb{R}^{d} \to \mathbb{R}</math> denotes the shifted and scaled version of <math>\varphi</math> given by
:<math>\varphi_{x}^{\lambda} (y) = \lambda^{-d} \varphi \left( \frac{y - x}{\lambda} \right)</math>.
